analysis.one_liner: Makes it easier to collect attorney's fees for winning civil rights claims without a final judgment.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with no cosponsors, was referred to the House Judiciary Committee in September 2026 and has had no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: When someone wins a civil rights lawsuit — say, against a police department or an employer that discriminated against them — federal law lets the court order the losing side to pay their attorney's fees. Since a 2001 Supreme Court decision, that has only worked if the win came as a final judgment or a signed settlement. This bill would broaden that: getting a preliminary court order, a written agreement, or even winning after the other side voluntarily fixed the problem would all count, so lawyers could be paid and people could afford to bring these cases. The bill went to the Judiciary Committee and has not moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who bring civil rights cases — workers facing discrimination, people suing police departments or government agencies, and renters or consumers with rights claims. It also makes their lawyers' work payable, which is what lets cases without big-dollar plaintiffs get filed at all.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Civil rights plaintiffs and their lawyers

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds a definition to the civil rights fee-shifting law (42 U.S.C. 1988) so a party counts as prevailing if it gets a court order — including a preliminary injunction or temporary restraining order — that materially changes the parties' relationship, even if the case later becomes moot.

It also counts enforceable written agreements or consent decrees, and situations where the defendant or a government agency voluntarily changed its position in a way that ended the case or granted the relief sought — the so-called 'catalyst' theory the Supreme Court rejected in 2001.
The bill applies to any case pending on, or filed after, the date it becomes law.

analysis.who_pays: Defendants in civil rights cases — businesses and employers accused of discrimination, state and local governments, and police departments — would face fee awards in more situations, and their insurers or taxpayers would often bear the cost.

drawbacks.text: Defendants who voluntarily fix a problem before a court rules could owe fees anyway, which critics argue pressures them to settle cases regardless of the underlying merits. This is the objection that led the Supreme Court to reject the catalyst theory in 2001.

Awarding fees based on preliminary orders, even ones later vacated on mootness grounds, could increase litigation costs for employers and governments, costs that may be passed to taxpayers or customers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would meaningfully lower the cost barrier to enforcing civil rights, which is real: fee-shifting is what makes many of these cases economically possible. The cost is more fee exposure for defendants and some added settlement pressure. The design largely restores pre-2001 practice rather than inventing something new, so the tradeoff is a familiar one that courts have litigated for decades.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Judiciary Committee, where it has sat with no cosponsors and no committee action so far.

narrative.text: Rep. Glenn Grothman (R-WI) introduced the bill on September 10, 2026.
It was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day, with no further action since.
No members have signed on as cosponsors.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: At this stage, defendants in civil rights suits — businesses, employers, and governments — are better off simply because the change has not advanced; with no cosponsors and a full committee agenda, its typical fate is to expire without a vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Defendants facing civil rights fee claims

for.name: Glenn Grothman
for.role: U.S. Representative, WI-6; introduced the bill
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee

sides.party_line_note: A single Republican introduced the bill with no cosponsors of either party, so no party split can be measured yet.

industries.industry: Employers and businesses defending discrimination and civil rights suits
industries.note: They would owe attorney's fees in more situations, including cases resolved by preliminary orders or their own voluntary changes. Their interest in the bill runs against the workers and individuals who bring those claims.

industries.industry: State and local governments, including police departments
industries.note: As the most common civil rights defendants, they would face more fee exposure, paid by taxpayers. Their interest in defeating the bill runs against the people suing them.

Fee recovery is what makes civil rights cases financially viable; broadening 'prevailing party' means more cases can be brought and paid. Their incentive aligns with ordinary people's access to court.

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors three months before the Congress ends and no committee action, the bill's realistic path is to expire without a markup or floor vote, like most introduced bills lacking visible support.
